theme: May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 20. It is a prayer for the king before he goes into battle. Read it as a congregation praying for its leader.
settingTheScene: Psalm 20 is a royal psalm “of David,” in which the people pray for the king as he goes out to war. The speakers shift between “we” and “I,” as the congregation prays and the king, or a priest, answers. David is now king, and the psalms of his kingship begin. After the long years of flight, the nation has a king whose success depends on God.
observation: “The LORD answer you in the day of trouble! The name of the God of Jacob protect you!” (v. 1).
“May he send you help from the sanctuary and give you support from Zion” (v. 2).
“May he remember all your offerings and regard with favor your burnt sacrifices” (v. 3).
“May he grant you your heart’s desire and fulfill all your plans!” (v. 4).
“May we shout for joy over your salvation, and in the name of our God set up our banners!” (v. 5).
“Now I know that the LORD saves his anointed; he will answer him from his holy heaven” (v. 6).
“Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (v. 7).
“O LORD, save the king! May he answer us when we call” (v. 9).
interpretation:
This psalm shows how a community prays for its leader. The people do not simply hope that the king will win. They ask the LORD to answer him, protect him, support him, and fulfill his plans. It is a model of intercessory prayer. A nation is stronger when its people pray for those who lead.

The psalm assumes that the king is a servant of God. His offerings are remembered. His plans are the plans God grants. Success is not the king’s alone. The people shout for joy over “your salvation,” but they raise their banners in “the name of our God.” The glory goes to God.

The turning point is verse 6. A voice declares, “Now I know that the LORD saves his anointed.” It is a statement of settled confidence. The prayer has been answered in the heart of the one who prays. This is common in the Psalms: prayer ends with certainty before the outcome is seen.

Verse 7 is the center of the psalm, and one of the most quoted lines in the Psalter. “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.” Chariots and horses were the superweapons of the ancient world. Israel was told never to multiply horses (Deuteronomy 17:16). The psalm declares that real security is found in God’s name, not in military power. In our time the chariots and horses may be money, technology, connections, or intelligence.

The closing line is a prayer that has become a national anthem for Israel: “O LORD, save the king!” In time, Israel’s kings would fail, and this prayer would point to the King who does not.
connection: The “anointed” of this psalm is the Messiah. Jesus was the king who went to battle against sin and death, and the Father heard him (Hebrews 5:7). “In the day of trouble” echoes his Gethsemane prayer. 1 Timothy 2:1-2 calls us to pray for kings and all in authority. Paul says that we trust “not in ourselves but in God who raises the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:9).
application:
Pray this psalm for a leader you know: a pastor, a boss, a government official.

Name your “chariots and horses,” the things you trust in apart from God.

Pray “O LORD, save the king” with Jesus in mind, who reigns now.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you trust in when trouble comes, and what you want to trust instead.
Ask him to answer those who lead you in the day of trouble.
Raise your banner in his name by telling him why you trust him.
